performers: Philharmonic Symphony Orchestra of London; Artur Rodzinski, conductor
intro: The fourth movement of the Symphony No. 5 in D minor, Op. 47, marked Allegro non troppo, ends with the brass in D major over a repeated high A. Rodzinski conducts a shortened version that cuts 37 bars from the finale.

sections.label: A · Brass march theme over timpani
sections.mNote: Trumpets, trombones and tuba play the march theme over timpani.

sections.label: B · Quiet violins
sections.mNote: The brass recede and the violins continue.

sections.label: Link · Low winds and drum
sections.mNote: Low woodwinds and drum lead into the return of the march.

sections.label: A′ · Brass over repeated string notes
sections.mNote: Brass phrases lengthen over repeated notes in the strings.

sections.label: Coda · D major, repeated A
sections.mNote: High repeated notes continue over sustained brass chords.

cues.title: Brass march over timpani
cues.text: After a full attack from woodwind and brass, trumpets, trombones and tuba play the march in D minor over the timpani. The strings rest.
cues.evidence: Shostakovich, Symphony No. 5, Muzgiz full score, plate M. 16313 Г, p. 109, rehearsal 97: Allegro non troppo, brass march and timpani; strings resting. https://imslp.tw/uploads/PMLASIA01319-Shostakovich_Fifth_Symphony%2C__Op__47_-_Full_Score.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Rodzinski’s 37-bar cut
cues.text: Rodzinski cut 37 bars from this finale. He made the same cut in his 1942 Cleveland recording and kept it in the Westminster version twelve years later.
cues.evidence: Niek Nelissen, review of Artur Rodzinski: Complete Westminster Recordings, August 2026, identifies a 37-bar cut in the 1942 recording and the same cut in the Westminster account. Its position in this transfer has not been established. https://www.opusklassiek.nl/cd-recensies/cd-nn/nnrodzinski_westminster.htm

cues.title: Violins after the march
cues.text: The brass grow softer and stop. The violins continue in a much quieter passage, playing small repeated figures above long notes in the lower parts.
cues.evidence: Muzgiz full score, pp. 138–142, from rehearsal 112: reduced dynamics and quieter violin writing after the opening march. The cut in this performance limits closer placement within this passage. https://imslp.tw/uploads/PMLASIA01319-Shostakovich_Fifth_Symphony%2C__Op__47_-_Full_Score.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Introduction to the score, 1956
cues.text: In the introduction to the 1956 Muzgiz score, published under his name, Shostakovich called the finale “an optimistic, invigorating outlet for all the tragic tensions of the earlier parts”.
cues.evidence: Introduction to the Score of Symphony No. 5, published under Shostakovich’s name by Muzgiz in 1956; text reproduced by DSCH Publishers. https://shostakovich-en.ru/140en

cues.title: Première, Leningrad, 21 November 1937
cues.text: At the première in Leningrad on 21 November 1937, the artist Lyubov Yakovleva watched Shostakovich respond to the applause. In her diary she described him as pale and biting his lips: “I think he might have burst into tears.”
cues.evidence: Lyubov Yakovleva’s diary account after the première of 21 November 1937, quoted in the DSCH Publishers work history. https://shostakovich-en.ru/140en

cues.title: Brass over repeated notes
cues.text: The march returns over repeated notes in the strings and woodwinds. Above this accompaniment the brass play longer phrases, and their note values lengthen towards the end.
cues.evidence: Muzgiz full score, pp. 156–158, rehearsals 130–131: repeated wind and string figures with longer brass phrases. https://imslp.tw/uploads/PMLASIA01319-Shostakovich_Fifth_Symphony%2C__Op__47_-_Full_Score.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Repeated A over D major
cues.text: High strings and woodwinds repeat A above long D major chords in the brass. The harmony underneath scarcely moves.
cues.evidence: Muzgiz full score, pp. 158–165: repeated A figures and the sustained D major close. https://imslp.tw/uploads/PMLASIA01319-Shostakovich_Fifth_Symphony%2C__Op__47_-_Full_Score.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Closing chords in D major
cues.text: The repeated notes stop. Brass and strings hold the closing D major chords, and the bass drum and timpani play repeated strokes beneath them.
cues.evidence: Muzgiz full score, p. 165: repeated-note figures cease before the final sustained chords; bass drum and timpani provide the closing accents. https://imslp.tw/uploads/PMLASIA01319-Shostakovich_Fifth_Symphony%2C__Op__47_-_Full_Score.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Violins continue after the brass chords
transitions.from: A · Brass march theme over timpani
transitions.how: The brass sustain their chords and diminish. At rehearsal 112 much of the orchestra stops, and the violins continue with repeated notes over a held bass. The tempo slows to crotchet = 80.
transitions.evidence: Muzgiz full score, p. 138, rehearsal 112. This describes the broad written withdrawal; the 37-bar cut prevents closer placement. https://imslp.tw/uploads/PMLASIA01319-Shostakovich_Fifth_Symphony%2C__Op__47_-_Full_Score.pdf

transitions.title: Repeated string figures and returning brass
transitions.to: A′ · Brass over repeated string notes
transitions.how: The passage for low wind and drums leads into repeated figures for the strings and upper woodwinds. Trumpets and trombones re-enter above them with longer phrases, and the bass supports the climb towards the closing D major.
transitions.evidence: Muzgiz full score, pp. 146–158, from rehearsal 121 to the later brass writing at rehearsals 130–131. https://imslp.tw/uploads/PMLASIA01319-Shostakovich_Fifth_Symphony%2C__Op__47_-_Full_Score.pdf

transitions.title: Repeated A over D major
transitions.from: A′ · Brass over repeated string notes
transitions.how: The repeated upper notes stay on A while the brass broaden into long chords. Underneath, the harmony is D major, with D in the bass. The strings continue their repeated notes through the sustained brass phrases up to the final orchestral chords.
transitions.evidence: Muzgiz full score, pp. 158–165: closing D major, repeated upper A and sustained brass and bass parts. https://imslp.tw/uploads/PMLASIA01319-Shostakovich_Fifth_Symphony%2C__Op__47_-_Full_Score.pdf

source.title: Symphony No. 5 — Muzgiz M. 16313 Г, historical full score
source.locator: Printed pp. 109–165; PDF pp. 111–167. The reported 37-bar cut (https://www.opusklassiek.nl/cd-recensies/cd-nn/nnrodzinski_westminster.htm) is not located; selected broad snapshots must not be read as an uncut bar map. Viewed score is public domain in Taiwan, not cleared for EU/US republication; exact performing edition unknown. Timing evidence: cache/analysis/shostakovich-5-finale.txt; source: https://archive.org/details/lp_symphony-no-5-opus-47_dmitri-shostakovich-philharmonic-symphony.

timeline.note: Opening wind/brass attack, then brass march with timpani, p. 109; strings rest at first. Successive opening events grouped, not one static chord.
Moving wind/string layers after the opening, p. 111 and following; approximate regional snapshot.
Reduced string region after the opening wave, p. 138; acoustic withdrawal near 3:16–3:20. Exact page-to-time correspondence remains uncertain because the cut is unaligned.
Selected rebuilding texture from p. 146/rehearsal 121, including side drum within percussion; approximate correspondence to the gradual late recovery, not an exact entrance.
Later orchestral accumulation, pp. 156–158; selected active groups, not an exhaustive chord inventory or an uncut timing map.
D-major closing section, pp. 164–165: repeated notes in the upper parts, long brass notes and bass support; approximate snapshot of the late coda.
Final sustained chords and percussion accents, p. 165. The last repeated-note attack and the final chords come one after the other in this closing excerpt.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Philharmonic Symphony Orchestra of London (orchestra), Artur Rodzinski (conductor)
fields.note: Original sleeve and labels establish the displayed credit. Later Westminster reissue documentation and the publisher’s discography identify the orchestra as the Royal Philharmonic Orchestra. That cross-identification is not substituted silently for the original label credit; individual players and soloists are not established.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Finale with a reported 37-bar performance cut; supplied digital track presented intact
fields.note: The cut is explicitly reported for the Westminster performance by the cited discographic review. Its exact bars and position in this transfer are not established. The historical full score is uncut; no missing passage is silently supplied, no alternative performance is substituted, and no local audio edit is made. Exact performing edition remains unknown.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: CiNii’s record for Westminster MVCW-18008 explicitly gives this range; the publisher independently lists the Rodzinski/Royal Philharmonic recording as 1954. Applying those reissue data to this differently credited LP is an inference. No original session ledger or precise movement-by-movement day has been located. 1956 is the selected LP’s publication year, not an invented session date.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: Venue transcribed exactly from the reissue catalogue record. The original LP does not supply a venue. Its linkage to the selected LP is the same qualified inference as the session-date attribution; no more specific hall name is invented.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: Original sleeve and labels; commercially issued Vinyl LP, Made in U.S.A. Sleeve ©1956 Westminster Recording Sales Corp.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: Both forms are visually present on the source object. These identify the selected 1956 issue, not an asserted first edition worldwide. The publisher lists an earlier 1955 Nixa issue of the attributed 1954 performance.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.value: Side 2: XTV 22721; movement 2 on that side
fields.note: Label matrix is legible in the scan. Side 1 contains Moderato/Allegretto; side 2 contains Largo/Allegro non troppo. Take numbers and faint runout/stamper suffixes are unknown and are not guessed.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: The explicit ripping_operator field is credited, not the different uploader/cataloguing operator. A separately named restoration engineer and original recording engineer are unknown.

fields.label: Transfer date

fields.label: Processing
fields.value: LP transfer: Technics SL1200MK5 / Audio-Technica AT95e → Radio Design Labs EZ-PH1 → Focusrite Scarlett 2i2; ArchiveCD 2.2.57lp; source-side 24-bit FLAC and Internet Archive VBR MP3 derivatives
fields.note: Hardware lineage and ripping software are explicit metadata. Original side FLAC tags say Processed by SoX; exact filtering, declicking, gain, speed calibration and derivative segmentation parameters are unknown. The sleeve’s Panorthophonic tape-recording and RIAA-mastering statements concern the original production, not a modern restoration recipe. No local speed correction, normalization, splice or replacement audio was applied.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Not cleared as public domain in the EU or US; composition rights remain separate from the historic recording basis
fields.note: Shostakovich died in 1975. The ordinary EU life-plus-70 calculation runs through 2045; this is not a global clearance or a statement of a US expiry date. IMSLP identifies the work as non-public-domain in the EU and US. The inspected score is territorially hosted as public domain in Taiwan and is cited, not republished. No composition licence is asserted.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 3: territorial EU historic-recording basis; commercial circulation documented by December 1955, selected LP issue dated 1956
fields.note: The original Westminster sleeve/labels and album metadata establish the selected 1956 WN 18001/XWN 18001 issue. A visually inspected High Fidelity review, December 1955, p. 80, already names this London orchestra, Rodzinski, his second recording of the Fifth and Westminster catalogue 18001; the review prints SWN 18001 and erroneously calls the symphony D major, so those details are not silently normalized. The publisher also lists Nixa WLP 20004 in 1955. First lawful publication anywhere before 1963 is the rule; no EU-first-release claim is required or made. source.rights.published 1956 remains a conservative upper bound tied to the selected physical issue, not a first-release date. Even using 1956, the ordinary 50-year recording term had expired before the 2013 extension. US sound-recording status is not established. Complete item metadata, original side-transfer provenance and scans disclose no Creative Commons non-commercial condition or separate upstream digital source. This is not a worldwide public-domain or composition-rights clearance.

composer.epithet: Composer of fifteen symphonies written under Soviet rule, who signed some of his most personal music with the four-note motif D–E♭–C–B♮.
facts: Petrograd Conservatory, 1919–25; Nikolayev for piano, Steinberg for composition
Leningrad from 1937; Moscow from 1943; both posts lost in 1948
D–E♭–C–B♮: DSCH in German note names
Fifteen symphonies and fifteen quartets; operas, concertos and cinema scores
composer.background:
For five weeks the cinema had been showing the same film, and Shostakovich had been playing the same accompaniment. “I’ve even started dreaming about this music,” he wrote from Leningrad to Boleslav Yavorsky on 18 October 1925. He was nineteen. His First Symphony was finished, but it was a graduation score and did not pay the household bills. His father had died three years earlier, and accompanying silent films helped to support the family.

He was born in St Petersburg in 1906 and learnt the piano from his mother, Sofiya. At the Petrograd Conservatory, which he entered in 1919, Leonid Nikolayev taught him piano and Maximilian Steinberg composition. Alexander Glazunov, the director, recognised his gifts and helped him through his student years. He graduated as a pianist in 1923 and as a composer in 1925.
